query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Thermally induced surface grain refinement in the FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating enhances high-temperature wear resistance and limits microscopic deformation by promoting a dynamic transition to an ultra‐nanocrystalline (or partially amorphous) near-surface layer during sliding.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating with a relatively coarse grain structure.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled thermal annealing treatment prior to operation to induce near-surface grain refinement.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding conditions (e.g., ≥600°C) under a defined applied load and sliding speed.
generation.structural_mediator: A dynamically formed ultra‐nanocrystalline or partially amorphous surface layer.
generation.mechanism: The thermal treatment refines the surface grain structure, lowering the activation energy required for dynamic amorphization during high-temperature sliding. This refined layer promotes an inverse Hall-Petch effect, which strengthens the surface and reduces wear and plastic deformation by limiting dislocation motion and grain boundary sliding.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline as-deposited coating, the thermally treated coating is predicted to exhibit a lower wear rate and less pronounced microscopic deformation, evidenced by fewer and less severe plastic deformation features on the worn surface.
generation.baseline: The standard as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating without thermal treatment.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected to be significant under high-temperature (≥600°C) sliding conditions and may not extend to lower temperatures or non-sliding wear environments.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal annealing parameters (temperature and duration) required to achieve a stable ultra‐nanocrystalline layer under prolonged high-temperature sliding remain uncertain, as does the long-term stability of the refined layer during cyclic loading.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coatings on a conventional metal substrate: one set remains as-deposited, and the other is subjected to a controlled thermal annealing treatment aimed at surface grain refinement. Subject both sets to high-temperature sliding tests (≥600°C) under identical loads and sliding speeds. Analyze the wear track using microscopy (SEM/TEM) and measure wear volume rates.
measurements: Surface grain size distribution via microscopy
Surface morphology and evidence of dynamic amorphization
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally treated coatings do not show a statistically significant reduction in wear volume and microscopic deformation, or if no evidence of an ultra-nanocrystalline/amorphous surface layer is observed compared to the as-deposited coatings, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The coating showed good wear resistance, with a volume wear rate of 0.38 ± 0.08 × 10−4 mm3·N−1·m−1, which makes it a promising coating for use in abrasive environments.

AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
